chapter: Playing, learning and the music's values
title: Recording live at the Vanguard with Earl Hines
summary: Playing with Earl Hines, Budd Johnson and Gene Ramey without rehearsal, and Hines's ring flying off.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: A couple of different recordings I wanted to ask you about. You played with Earl Hines?

Oh that was something. That “Live at the Vanguard.” That’s one of my favorite things that I made. It was almost the same kind of thing. He was the nicest man. The nicest guy. I mean whooh. He was the nicest person, oh man. And we never rehearsed. I never rehearsed with him either. It was Budd Johnson and Gene Ramey, we played with him. That was quite an experience. He was dynamic. He was so dynamic on that piano, it was just like whooh. It was like a whole band. You never knew what he was going to do. You had to really stay on your toes, especially a drummer, because his thing was, he was all between the beat and all kinds of things when he played. I remember one time we went down to Washington, D.C. and he was striding — his ring just came off his finger and went out into the audience.

I mean his left hand was just working so hard man. See that’s like when those guys played, they were in it. And his ring come off. Oh, that was amazing. That’s why I say I was just about the luckiest guy like that, that had those experiences with that caliber of people, not only as musicians but as people too.
